blocks.text: There is, however, an island opposite Tripoli in Syria which took its name from the rabbits that are frequent there (Canincheninsel); see Maundrell, Travels p. 31. Oedmann, Vermischte Sammlungen fasc. 4, ch. 5, p. 49, thinks that they are not native there but were brought there from elsewhere. Russell, Natur. History of Aleppo p. 55, attests that at Aleppo a few rabbits are kept for the table by the Europeans living there. From this, however, it is not established with certainty whether these animals are native to that region.
This reason for the name seems to have escaped a certain learned man in the Notes on Bruce's Travels, edited by Hassencamp, p. 159, 60.

In this Stumpf undoubtedly erred. For everyone knows that the marmot is an animal peculiar to the Savoyard, Swiss and Pyrenean Alps. Nor has any of those who have visited the regions of the East found that animal there. But the animals that Stumpf thinks are like Alpine mice in Egypt seem to be the Syrian hyraces or sorices, the ἔχινοι χερσαῖοι [echinoi chersaioi] of Aelian (book 3, ch. 10, where their foresight and skill in storing away food are recounted; cf. Bochart below, p. 1008. 3, and p. 1016), in which we find everything that the Arabs relate of the وبر [wabr]. The animal has the size of a marmot, but a more elongated body; the back is marked with bristles projecting from the ridge (from which the Greeks undoubtedly gave it the name ἐχῖνος [echinos]); it is dark above and whitish below; the snout is oblong; the claws very short; there is no tail; its gait is creeping, its diet vegetable; it lives in the hollows of rocks. See Schreber, Mammalia 4, pl. 211. B. Shaw described this animal under the name of lamb of Israel (see Bochart above) (Travels p. 301, German trans., where, however, Daman Israel is wrongly written for Ganam Israel غنم اسرايل [ghanam isrāyl], an error that has crept into many other books); he found the animal frequent on Mount Lebanon and in other places of Syria. It was also known to Prosper Alpinus, who mentioned a certain low animal, not unlike a rabbit, which they call the lamb of Israel, in Hist. Nat. Aegypti vol. 1, ch. 20, p. 80, and book 4, ch. 9. Shaw, loc. cit., was the first to contend that the Hebrew name of this Syrian hyrax was שפן. He has recently found an ally in Bruce, Travels vol. 5, p. 149, Leipzig trans., who carefully describes this animal, which he saw frequently not only in Syria but also in Ethiopia, under the name Aschkoko, by which it is known among the Amharas, from the bristles projecting from the ridge of its back like thorns (for the Amharic Aschok means thorn: see Ludolf, Lexic. Amhar. p. 58). He also gave an illustration of it, plate 29. And it must be admitted that everything we read in the Hebrew text about the שפן is found in the Syrian hyrax, the وبر [wabr]. First, neither is cloven-footed. 2. Both chew the cud; Bruce, l. p. 148, attests that he observed this in the Aschkoko, that is, a hyrax, which he kept at home; cf. Levit. XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7. 3. Both are edible, though unclean: the flesh of the Syrian hyrax is eaten by those Arabs who live on Lebanon and in Arabia Petraea (see the words of Mavardius quoted by Bochart above), although the other Muslims and the Abyssinian Christians abstain from it as from an unclean food. See Bruce p. 151. 4. Both are gregarious, Bruce p. 146; cf. Prov. XXX, 26. 5. Both are feeble, Prov. loc. cit. 6. Both have their home in the rock, Shaw p. 301, Bruce p. 146; cf. Ps. CIV, 18. 7. Both are frequent in Syria and Eretz Yisrael, on the testimony of those same travellers. Yet we shall find every one of these points in the jerboa (mus iaculus) as well, the يربوع [yarbūʿ] of the Arabs, about which Bochart says much in what follows.

Bruce described this animal far more accurately than the Arabs, vol. 5, p. 144, Leipzig trans. It appears to be a species of viverra, which Blumenbach, in a note on that passage of Bruce, calls viverra aurita on account of its remarkable oval ears. The name of the animal was unknown to Buffon, who gave a description of it in the Supplements to vol. 3 of the Hist. Nat.

But if the وبر [wabr] is the hyrax Syriacus (and we think this has been sufficiently proved above, note 3), nothing will prevent the وبر [wabr] of the Arabs and the שפן of the Hebrews from being the same animal.

Mus jaculus with an elongated tufted tail, nearly five-toed fore-paws, very long thighs, very short arms, Linnaeus, Systema Naturae vol. 1, p. 157, ed. 13. Descriptions of the animal, which they had carefully observed, were given by Hasselquist in Itinerar. Palaestinae p. 277, by Pallas in Novis Specieb. Quadruped. ex Glirium ordine p. 277 ff., and by Bruce in Travels vol. 5, p. 128 ff. With these should be compared Oedmann in the Vermischten Sammlungen fasc. 4, p. 48.
